props.title: Bird People in China

sections.content: The Bird People in China (1998) represents a fascinating departure for director Takashi Miike, known primarily for shocking yakuza films like Audition (1999) and Ichi the Killer (2001). This gentle, meditative drama follows a Japanese salaryman into remote China, where ancient myths of winged people collide with modernization. It shares spiritual DNA with Werner Herzog's Wings of Hope (1998) and Little Buddha (1993) in its exploration of isolated cultures facing extinction. Miike trades his signature violence for contemplative beauty, creating a bridge between Japanese corporate culture and vanishing traditions.

sections.content: The film connects to a broader 1990s movement exploring Asia's rapid industrialization through a mystical lens. Seven Years in Tibet (1997) and The Cup (1999) similarly examine the collision between tradition and progress, though Miike's approach is uniquely dreamlike. His camera lingers on mist-shrouded mountains and village rituals with the same patience he typically reserves for yakuza violence, creating an elegiac tone that recalls Spring Summer Fall Winter... and Spring (2003).

While ostensibly about China, the film serves as Miike's meditation on Japan's own modernization and lost traditions. The salaryman protagonist mirrors Japan's post-war transformation, much like how After Life (1998) and Maborosi (1995) use supernatural elements to process cultural change. The mythical bird people become a metaphor for vanishing ways of life, similar to the forest spirits in Princess Mononoke (1997). SUBHEAD: Cultural Preservation vs. Progress

movies.title: The Road Home
movies.slug: Zhang Yimou's touching story of a businessman returning to his rural Chinese village

sections.content: Like The Last Emperor (1987) and Farewell My Concubine (1993), The Bird People in China grapples with the price of progress. But where those films take sweeping historical views, Miike keeps his focus intimate and current. The businessman's journey from skeptic to believer mirrors films like Why Has Bodhi-Dharma Left for the East? (1989), where modern characters confront ancient wisdom. The film's bittersweet ending suggests that some cultural loss is inevitable in modernization, but memory and myth endure.
